title: The Man Who Waited Beside a Pool for 38 Years
paragraphs:
The Man Who Waited Beside a Pool for 38 Years
Thirty-Eight Years of Waiting. One Question from Jesus Changed Everything.
For thirty-eight years, he woke up to the same disappointment.
Thirty-eight years.

Longer than some marriages.
Longer than many careers.
Longer than some people live.
Every morning he opened his eyes hoping something would change.
Every night he closed them carrying the same unanswered prayer.
And maybe that is why his story feels so personal.
Because most of us know what it feels like to wait.
Not beside a pool in Jerusalem.
But beside a broken marriage.
A doctor's report.
A financial struggle.
A grieving heart.
An addiction we thought would be gone by now.
A prayer that feels lost somewhere between earth and heaven.
We know what it feels like to sit beside something for years and wonder if God has forgotten us.
That is where we meet him in John chapter 5.
Not standing.
Not celebrating.
Not victorious.
Just waiting.
The Apostle John writes:
The name Bethesda likely comes from the Aramaic expression Beth Hesda, meaning "House of Mercy."
Think about that.
A man who desperately needed mercy was lying beside a place literally called the House of Mercy.
Yet year after year he remained unchanged.
Sometimes people can sit beside mercy and never enter it.
Sometimes people can sit beside church, beside Scripture, beside Christian content, beside truth itself, and still never surrender to Christ.
The tragedy is not always being far from God.
Sometimes it is being near Him without truly coming to Him.
John continues:
"One man was there who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years." (John 5:5)
Thirty-eight years.
Scripture intentionally repeats the number because God wants us to feel the weight of it.
The Hebrew mind understood long waiting.
Israel wandered the wilderness for decades because of unbelief.
Entire generations lived and died before seeing God's promises fulfilled.
Waiting was never merely about time.
Waiting revealed the condition of the heart.
And this man's waiting had become his identity.
Have you ever noticed how suffering can become part of who we think we are?
We stop saying:
"I am struggling."
And start saying:
"This is just who I am."
We stop saying:
"I have a problem."
And start saying:
"I will always be this way."
The longer pain stays, the more permanent it feels.
Then Jesus arrived.
Not because the man called for Him.
Not because the man had extraordinary faith.
Not because he deserved a miracle.
Jesus simply stepped into the scene.
Because grace always arrives before we deserve it.
That is the story of the Gospel.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God demonstrates His own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
Grace does not wait for worthiness.
Grace creates transformation.
Jesus looked at the man and asked a question that sounds almost absurd.
In Greek, the Lord asks:
"Θέλεις ὑγιὴς γενέσθαι;" (Theleis hygiēs genesthai?)
"Do you want to be made well?" (John 5:6)
At first glance the question feels strange.
Of course he wanted to be healed.
Why else would he be there?
But Jesus was reaching deeper than physical paralysis.
He was exposing something hidden.
When disappointment lasts long enough, people can become attached to their excuses.
When suffering lasts long enough, people can become comfortable with hopelessness.
Healing changes everything.
Healing requires movement.
Healing requires responsibility.
Healing requires faith.
Jesus was asking:
Do you truly want a different life?
The man's answer is heartbreaking.
He says:
"Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up." (John 5:7)
Notice what he did not say.
He did not answer the question.
Instead, he explained why nothing had changed.
For thirty-eight years he had accumulated reasons.
Excuses.
Pain.
Disappointments.
Failures.
And perhaps some bitterness.
How often do we do the same?
Jesus asks for faith.
We offer explanations.
Jesus offers freedom.
We describe our limitations.
Jesus points toward possibility.
We point toward our history.
The man believed his future was trapped by his circumstances.
But Jesus never needed the pool.
Because the source of healing was standing right in front of him.
Many people are still waiting for a pool.
A better opportunity.
A different season.
More money.
More influence.
A perfect church.
A perfect family.
A perfect moment.
Meanwhile Jesus is saying:
"I am already here."
Then came one of the most powerful commands in Scripture.
Jesus said:
"Get up, take up your bed, and walk." (John 5:8)
In Greek:
"Ἔγειρε, ἆρον τὸν κράβαττόν σου καὶ περιπάτει."
"Egeire, aron ton krabatton sou kai peripatei."

Rise.
Pick up what once carried you.
Walk.
No ceremony.
No dramatic countdown.
No ritual.
Just the authority of the Son of God.
And instantly everything changed.
The text says:
"At once the man was healed, and he took up his bed and walked." (John 5:9)
At once.
Thirty-eight years of suffering.
One moment with Jesus.
The same power that spoke galaxies into existence spoke life into a broken body.
Because Jesus is not merely a teacher.
He is not merely a prophet.
He is not merely a moral example.
He is the eternal Son of God.
The Word made flesh.
The One whom John introduced in Greek as:
"Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ Λόγος"
"In the beginning was the Word." (John 1:1)
The Logos.
The Creator.
The Redeemer.
The Savior.
And this miracle points to something far greater than physical healing.
The real story is not a healed body.
The real story is a picture of salvation.
Because every one of us was spiritually helpless.
Unable to save ourselves.
Unable to heal ourselves.
Unable to remove our own sin.
Ephesians 2:1 says we were dead in our trespasses and sins.
Dead people do not rescue themselves.
Jesus came for people who could not save themselves.
People like the man at Bethesda.
People like me.
People like you.
Maybe that is why this story continues to grip hearts two thousand years later.
Because beneath the details of Jerusalem and pools and miracles, we recognize ourselves.
Some of us have spent years waiting.
Years carrying regret.
Years hiding shame.
Years believing we are too broken.
Too sinful.
Too far gone.
But the Gospel announces a different verdict.
The cross declares that no scandal is greater than God's grace.
No failure is stronger than Christ's redemption.
No past is more powerful than His mercy.
The enemy wants you to believe your story is finished.
Jesus specializes in rewriting endings.
That is exactly what happened beside the pool.
A forgotten man became a living testimony.
A hopeless story became a Gospel story.
A scandal of suffering became a display of grace.
Maybe today you feel like the man beside Bethesda.
Maybe you are exhausted.
Maybe your faith feels weak.
Maybe your heart carries wounds nobody sees.
Maybe you have waited so long that disappointment feels normal.
Listen carefully.
Jesus has not forgotten you.
The same Savior who walked through Jerusalem still walks into impossible situations.
The same Savior who spoke life to a broken man still speaks life today.
The same Savior who rewrote his story can rewrite yours.
And perhaps that is why you were meant to read this article.
Not merely to admire the miracle.
But to meet the Miracle Worker.
If this message stirred something inside you, do not keep scrolling.
Your testimony may encourage someone who feels completely alone right now.
Because one encounter with Jesus can redeem what decades of pain could never fix.
